content_review.notes: Phase 0b skeleton: shared immediate-relative journey structure, category-neutral USCIS / NVC steps reused, parent-specific content removed. Legal content is pending qualified U.S. immigration legal review. See docs/ir2-implementation-plan.md.

chapters.chapter_description: U.S. citizen petitioner files Form I-130 to establish qualifying relationship with child

actions: Verify the petitioner is a U.S. citizen
Identify the qualifying parent-child relationship
Confirm the child is unmarried and under 21
Check relationship-specific rules for a father, stepparent, or adoptive parent
Confirm core relationship evidence is available

steps.step_description: Check whether the petitioner and the child qualify for an IR-2 immigrant visa petition. The child must be unmarried and under 21, and the petitioner must be the child's U.S. citizen parent, stepparent, or adoptive parent under U.S. immigration law.

quest_data.title: Determine Eligibility
quest_data.subtitle: Before filing, confirm that the U.S. citizen petitioner, the parent-child relationship, and the child meet the core conditions for an IR-2 child petition. Complete each section below.

quests.title: Petitioner is the child's U.S. citizen parent
quests.subtitle: Confirm the petitioner can file an IR-2 petition for a child

screens.label: Petitioner Status
screens.question: What is the petitioner's current U.S. immigration or citizenship status?
screens.helper: Only a U.S. citizen parent can file in the IR-2 category. A green card holder parent files for a child in a different, preference category (F-2A), which this journey does not cover.

options.label: Lawful Permanent Resident (green card holder)
options.sub: A green card holder parent cannot file an IR-2 petition. The child may qualify in the F-2A category instead.

screens.label: How Citizenship Was Obtained
screens.question: How did the petitioner become a U.S. citizen?
screens.helper: Citizenship by birth, acquisition, derivation, or naturalization may qualify. Select the path that applies.

options.label: Born abroad and acquired or derived U.S. citizenship

screens.label: Proof of Citizenship
screens.question: Does the petitioner have accepted proof of U.S. citizenship?
screens.helper: The petitioner generally needs one valid document proving U.S. citizenship.

items: U.S. birth certificate
Valid or previously issued U.S. passport
Certificate of Naturalization
Certificate of Citizenship
Consular Report of Birth Abroad

options.label: Yes, at least one accepted document is available
Not yet, but it can be obtained
No, and obtaining proof may be difficult

screens.label: Identity Consistency
screens.question: Do the petitioner's citizenship records and the child's birth record show the petitioner's name the same way?
screens.helper: Differences may be explainable, but legal name-change or discrepancy evidence should be prepared before filing.

options.label: There is a difference, but legal supporting evidence is available
There is a difference and supporting evidence is not available yet

Continue to the child section." }; })()

quests.title: The child qualifies as a child under immigration law
quests.subtitle: Confirm the relationship, the child's age, and the child's marital status

screens.label: Relationship to the Petitioner
screens.question: How is the child related to the U.S. citizen petitioner?
screens.helper: The evidence and legal rules differ for a biological child, a stepchild, and an adopted child.

options.label: The petitioner is the child's biological mother
The petitioner is the child's biological father, and the parents were married to each other when the child was born
The petitioner is the child's biological father, and the parents were not married to each other when the child was born
The petitioner is the child's stepparent
The petitioner is a guardian, foster parent, or relative without a qualifying legal relationship

screens.label: Child's Age
screens.question: How old is the child today?
screens.helper: IR-2 is for an unmarried child under 21. For an immediate relative child like IR-2, the Child Status Protection Act locks the child's age on the date the I-130 is filed. So the child must be under 21 on the filing date, and must stay unmarried.

options.label: 18, 19, or 20
options.sub: File as early as possible. Do not wait until close to the 21st birthday.

options.label: 21 or older
options.sub: A son or daughter aged 21 or older does not qualify as IR-2 unless an I-130 was already filed before the 21st birthday.

screens.label: Marital Status
screens.question: Has the child ever been married?
screens.helper: IR-2 is only for an unmarried child. If the child marries before immigrating, the child no longer qualifies as IR-2.

options.label: No, the child has never been married
Yes, the child is married now
options.sub: A married son or daughter of a U.S. citizen does not qualify as IR-2.

options.label: The child was married before, but the marriage has ended
options.sub: Confirm the child's current unmarried status with official divorce or death records.

screens.label: Birth Record
screens.question: Does the child's birth certificate name the petitioner as a parent?
screens.helper: A birth record naming the petitioner is primary relationship evidence in most IR-2 cases. Stepchild and adoption cases also need the marriage or adoption records.

options.label: Yes, the petitioner is correctly named
The petitioner is named, but there are spelling, date, or identity differences
No, the petitioner is not named

screens.label: Relationship Authenticity
screens.question: Is the claimed parent-child relationship genuine and supported by truthful civil or family records?
screens.helper: USCIS requires a real qualifying relationship. False parentage, altered records, or material misrepresentation can cause denial and serious immigration consequences.

options.label: Yes, the relationship and records are genuine
There may be inaccurate or conflicting information in the records
No, the claimed relationship is not legally or factually genuine

companion_tool.title: Will your child turn 21 soon?
companion_tool.body: If the I-130 is filed before the child turns 21, the child's age is locked on that day. Check the last date to file.

quests.title: Relationship-specific requirements are satisfied
quests.subtitle: Check the rules for a father, a stepparent, an adoptive parent, and custody

screens.label: Parents' Marriage
screens.question: If the petitioner is the child's biological father, were the child's parents married to each other when the child was born?
screens.helper: For a father's petition, the parents' marriage changes what evidence is needed. Select not applicable for a mother, stepparent, or adoption case.

options.label: Yes, the parents were legally married
No, the parents were not legally married
Not applicable, this is not a biological-father case

screens.label: Legitimation
screens.question: If the parents were not married, was the child legally legitimated before turning 18, while the child was in the legal custody of the legitimating parent?
screens.helper: Legitimation is a legal act under the law of the child's or the father's place of residence or domicile, for example the parents marrying each other later. It is one of two routes for a father whose child was born to unmarried parents. If it does not apply, the next question covers the other route.

options.label: Yes, the child was legitimated before 18 while in the father's legal custody
No, or the child was not legitimated in time
Not applicable, the parents were married or this is not a biological-father case

screens.label: Father-Child Relationship
screens.question: If the child was not legitimated, did a genuine father-child relationship exist before the child's 21st birthday, while the child was unmarried?
screens.helper: Evidence may include the father's financial support, his involvement in the child's welfare and upbringing, his recognition of the child as his own, living together or regular contact, and school, medical or family records that show his role.

options.label: Yes, a genuine father-child relationship existed before 21
Not applicable, the child was legitimated, the parents were married, or this is not a biological-father case

screens.label: Stepparent Marriage Timing
screens.question: If the petitioner is the child's stepparent, did the petitioner marry the child's parent before the child turned 18?
screens.helper: The marriage that creates the step-relationship must have happened before the child's 18th birthday.

options.label: Yes, the marriage happened before the child turned 18
No, the marriage happened on or after the child's 18th birthday
Not applicable, this is not a stepchild case

screens.label: Length of the Stepparent Marriage
screens.question: If the petitioner is the stepparent, will the marriage to the child's parent be at least 2 years old when the child receives the visa?
screens.helper: When the parents' marriage is less than 2 years old, the child may receive a conditional (CR-2) visa instead of IR-2, with a later step to remove the conditions. Confirm this on the official sources for your case.

options.label: Yes, the marriage will be 2 years old or more
No, the marriage will be less than 2 years old
options.sub: The child may be issued a CR-2 visa. CR-2 has its own rules, which Rahvana shows separately.

options.label: Not applicable, this is not a stepchild case

screens.label: Adoption Timing
screens.question: If the petitioner adopted the child, how old was the child when the adoption was completed?
screens.helper: An adopted child generally qualifies only if the adoption was completed before the child turned 16. A narrow exception allows an adoption before 18 for a natural sibling of another child the same parent or parents adopted under the qualifying rules. The next question checks that exception.

options.label: Not applicable, this is not an adoption case

screens.label: Adopted Sibling Exception
screens.question: If the adoption was completed at 16 or 17, is the child the natural sibling of another child adopted by the same parent or parents under the qualifying adoption rules?
screens.helper: This exception is narrow and the custody and residence rules still apply. If it may apply, have a qualified U.S. immigration attorney review the case before filing.

options.label: Yes, a natural sibling was adopted by the same parent or parents
Not applicable, the adoption was before 16 or this is not an adoption case

screens.label: Adoption Custody and Residence
screens.question: If the petitioner adopted the child, has the child been in the petitioner's legal custody for at least 2 years, and lived with the petitioner for at least 2 years, before or after the adoption?
screens.helper: Both 2-year requirements must be met, and the time can come before or after the adoption. Check the custody period and the time living together separately, because each needs its own evidence.

options.label: No, one or both are not met
Not applicable, this is not an adoption case

screens.label: Adoption or Guardianship
screens.question: If the petitioner adopted the child, is there a final adoption decree, or is the arrangement a guardianship order (for example under Pakistan's Guardians and Wards Act)?
screens.helper: Guardianship (for example a guardianship order from a Pakistani court) is not automatically treated as an adoption for IR-2. If the child is in your care under guardianship, speak with a qualified U.S. immigration attorney before filing.

options.label: There is a final adoption decree
It is a guardianship order
options.sub: Guardianship is not automatically an adoption for IR-2. Speak with a qualified U.S. immigration attorney before filing.

options.label: Not applicable, this is not an adoption case

screens.label: Custody and the Other Parent
screens.question: If the child's parents are divorced or separated, is there a custody order or written consent from the other parent?
screens.helper: The consulate may ask for custody papers or the other parent's consent before issuing a visa to a minor. Confirm what the embassy requires for your case.

options.label: Yes, a custody order or written consent is available
Not applicable, the parents live together or this does not apply

quests.title: Core relationship evidence can be documented
quests.subtitle: Confirm that the petitioner can prove the qualifying parent-child relationship

screens.label: Primary Relationship Documents
screens.question: Which primary relationship records are currently available?
screens.helper: Select all that apply. The exact combination depends on the relationship type.

options.label: Child's birth certificate naming the petitioner
None of these are currently available

screens.label: Secondary Evidence
screens.question: If a primary record is unavailable or inconsistent, is credible secondary evidence available?
screens.helper: Secondary evidence may help when a civil record is unavailable, late-registered, or inconsistent. USCIS may also ask for more evidence or suggest DNA testing in some cases.

options.label: School, medical, vaccination, or religious records
Financial support, photographs, or proof of living together
Affidavits from people with personal knowledge of the birth
Not needed, complete primary evidence is available

screens.label: Translations
screens.question: Are complete English translations available for documents that are not in English?
screens.helper: Any foreign-language document submitted to USCIS must include a full English translation with the translator's certification of competence and accuracy.

options.label: Yes, translations are complete and certified
Not yet, translations can be prepared
Not applicable, all records are in English

quests.title: Additional IR-2 planning and visa ineligibility screening
quests.subtitle: Screen for common admissibility, sponsorship, domicile, and case-structure concerns

screens.label: Child's Immigration History
screens.question: Has the child ever been refused a U.S. visa, denied an immigration benefit, removed, deported, ordered to leave, or accused of fraud or misrepresentation?
screens.helper: A prior refusal does not automatically prevent approval, but fraud, removal, or misrepresentation may create serious legal issues.

screens.label: Criminal History
screens.question: Has the child ever been arrested, charged, convicted, or involved in a criminal case anywhere in the world?
screens.helper: Even old, dismissed, or juvenile cases may need to be disclosed and documented.

options.label: Yes, at least one incident exists

screens.label: Prior U.S. Presence
screens.question: Has the child ever entered the United States without inspection, overstayed, worked without authorization, or violated U.S. immigration status?
screens.helper: Some violations may affect eligibility. Special rules can apply to time spent in the U.S. as a minor, so get advice if any of these apply.

screens.label: Health and Vaccination
screens.question: Is there a known medical, communicable-disease, or vaccination issue that may come up during the immigrant visa medical exam?
screens.helper: The panel physician performs the required medical examination, checks the vaccinations that apply to the child, and sends the medical results to the consular officer. The consular officer decides visa eligibility after reviewing the medical report and other records. A health condition does not automatically mean the child is ineligible.

options.label: Yes, a medical or vaccination concern may come up

screens.label: Financial Sponsorship
screens.question: Can the petitioner likely submit Form I-864 and meet the financial sponsorship requirement through income, assets, household income, or a joint sponsor?
screens.helper: The petitioner generally must submit Form I-864. Some children may be exempt if they will automatically become U.S. citizens upon admission under the Child Citizenship Act. This depends on the child's age, admission as a permanent resident, and the custody and citizenship requirements, so check the individual case before relying on it. Financial sponsorship is handled mainly at the NVC stage, but planning should start now.

options.label: Possibly, a joint sponsor or assets may be needed
No, no viable sponsorship plan is currently available

screens.label: U.S. Domicile
screens.question: Does the petitioner live in the U.S., or have a concrete plan to establish or re-establish U.S. domicile no later than the date the child is admitted to the U.S. as a permanent resident?
screens.helper: A petitioner living abroad may still file Form I-130. However, the petitioner must establish or re-establish U.S. domicile no later than the date the child is admitted to the United States as a lawful permanent resident.

options.label: Petitioner lives abroad but has a documented plan to re-establish domicile
No, there is currently no U.S. domicile plan

screens.label: Separate Petition for Each Child
screens.question: If more than one child will immigrate, is the petitioner prepared to file a separate Form I-130 for each child?
screens.helper: Each child needs a separate I-130. Rahvana tracks each child as a separate journey.

options.label: Yes, only one child is immigrating or separate petitions will be filed
No, we expected one petition to cover several children

steps.notes: The petitioner must be the child's U.S. citizen parent. The child must be unmarried and under 21 and qualify as the petitioner's child under U.S. immigration law. Each child needs a separate Form I-130 and IR-2 case.

risk_signals.disclaimer: Educational screening based on USCIS and Department of State requirements. It is not an official USCIS or consular eligibility determination and is not legal advice. Pending review by a qualified U.S. immigration attorney.

patterns.title: Petitioner is not a U.S. citizen
patterns.advisory: Only a U.S. citizen parent can file an IR-2 petition. A green card holder parent files for an unmarried child in the F-2A category.

patterns.title: Child is married
patterns.advisory: IR-2 is only for an unmarried child. A married son or daughter of a U.S. citizen files in the F-3 category. If the child marries before immigrating, the IR-2 case ends.

patterns.title: Child is 21 or older
patterns.advisory: A son or daughter aged 21 or older does not qualify as IR-2 unless an I-130 was filed before the 21st birthday. Confirm the filing date and the age rule.

patterns.title: Child is close to 21
patterns.advisory: File the I-130 as soon as possible. For immediate relatives, the child's age is generally fixed on the filing date.

patterns.title: Birth record is missing or inconsistent
patterns.advisory: Obtain the correct civil birth record if available. If it is unavailable or inconsistent, prepare record-unavailability evidence, NADRA CRC / FRC records, other early records, and a clear explanation of the differences.
patterns.source_basis: Form I-130 Instructions; USCIS Policy Manual Vol. 6, Part B

patterns.title: Father's petition for a child born outside marriage
patterns.advisory: Gather legitimation evidence (legitimated before 18 while in the father's legal custody) or proof of a genuine father-child relationship that existed before the child turned 21 while unmarried. These cases need relationship-specific evidence.

patterns.title: Step-relationship created after age 18
patterns.advisory: The marriage that creates the step-relationship must happen before the child turns 18. A later marriage does not create an IR-2 stepchild relationship.

patterns.title: Child may receive a conditional CR-2 visa
patterns.advisory: When the parents' marriage is less than 2 years old at the time of admission, the child may receive conditional residence (CR-2) and must later apply to remove the conditions.

patterns.title: Adoption age, custody, or residence requirements are not established
patterns.advisory: An adoption-based IR-2 petition generally requires an adoption before age 16 (or before 18 under the narrow sibling exception), plus 2 years of legal custody and 2 years of living together. Get specialist legal review before filing if any part is uncertain.

patterns.title: Guardianship order instead of an adoption decree
patterns.advisory: Guardianship (for example a guardianship order from a Pakistani court) is not automatically treated as an adoption for IR-2. If the child is in your care under guardianship, speak with a qualified U.S. immigration attorney before filing.

patterns.title: Petitioner is only a guardian, foster parent, or relative
patterns.advisory: Guardianship, foster care, financial support, or raising a child does not by itself create a qualifying parent-child relationship for IR-2.

patterns.title: Custody papers or other parent's consent may be missing
patterns.advisory: The consulate may ask for a custody order or the other parent's written consent for a minor. Check the embassy's current requirements and prepare the papers early.
patterns.source_basis: Department of State immigrant visa guidance (pending confirmation)

patterns.title: Several children expected to use one petition
patterns.advisory: File a separate Form I-130 for each child. IR-2 has no derivative beneficiaries.
patterns.source_basis: Form I-130 filing structure; immediate-relative classification rules

patterns.title: Child has prior removal, fraud, or misrepresentation history
patterns.advisory: Obtain all prior decisions, visa records, removal documents, and immigration filings. Fraud or willful misrepresentation may create a permanent inadmissibility ground unless a waiver is available.

patterns.title: Child has an arrest, charge, or conviction
patterns.advisory: Collect certified court and police records for every incident and get legal analysis before filing or consular processing.

patterns.title: Child has U.S. presence or status-violation history
patterns.advisory: Some U.S. presence or status violations can affect eligibility. Review the full entry, exit, and status history with a qualified attorney before choosing consular processing.

patterns.title: Financial sponsorship may be insufficient
patterns.advisory: The petitioner generally must submit Form I-864. If income is not enough, review assets, household income, or a joint sponsor. A joint sponsor does not replace the petitioner's own I-864.

patterns.title: Petitioner may not meet U.S. domicile
patterns.advisory: A petitioner living abroad must show U.S. domicile, or concrete steps to re-establish it, no later than the child's admission as a permanent resident.

steps.where: USCIS, U.S. vital-record offices, Pakistani civil authorities, and other issuing authorities
actions: Get the petitioner's proof of U.S. citizenship
Get the child's Birth Registration Certificate (Union Council or local authority) naming the petitioner
Get the child's NADRA CRC (B-Form) as supporting evidence
Add the parents' Nikah Nama and MRC, legitimation evidence, stepparent marriage records, or adoption decree, as your case needs
Prepare custody papers or the other parent's consent if the parents are divorced or separated
Order certified English translations for non-English documents
Check the current I-130 instructions at uscis.gov for the required document list
stageWarnings: Do not obtain time-sensitive police or medical documents unnecessarily early.
steps.step_short_description: Relationship and civil documents for an IR-2 child petition
steps.step_description: Before filing Form I-130, collect the documents that prove the petitioner's U.S. citizenship and the qualifying parent-child relationship. Which relationship documents you need depends on whether the child is a biological child, a stepchild, or an adopted child. Guardianship (for example a guardianship order from a Pakistani court) is not automatically treated as an adoption for IR-2. If the child is in your care under guardianship, speak with a qualified U.S. immigration attorney before filing. Documents not in English need a certified English translation.

document_items.name: Proof of U.S. Citizenship
document_items.subtitle: Establishes that the petitioner is a U.S. citizen who can file an IR-2 petition for a child

document_items.name: Child's Birth Certificate
document_items.subtitle: Birth Registration Certificate from the Union Council, Municipal Corporation, CDA or Cantonment Board, naming the petitioner as the child's parent

document_items.name: Child Registration Certificate (CRC / B-Form)
document_items.subtitle: NADRA-issued record that links the child to both parents. It supports the birth certificate and can serve as alternate evidence if the birth record is late or missing; it does not replace it

document_items.name: Parents' Marriage Certificate (Nikah Nama and MRC)
document_items.subtitle: Needed when a father files and the parents were married. For a Muslim marriage, the MRC usually comes from the local Union Council, Municipal Corporation, CDA or Cantonment Board

document_items.name: Legitimation or Father-Child Relationship Evidence
document_items.subtitle: Needed when a father files for a child whose parents were not married to each other

document_items.name: Marriage Certificate Creating the Step-Relationship
document_items.subtitle: Shows the petitioner married the child's parent before the child turned 18

document_items.name: Termination of Prior Marriages
document_items.subtitle: Divorce or death records showing that earlier marriages of the petitioner and the child's parent ended first

document_items.name: Final Adoption Decree
document_items.subtitle: Court decree of a full adoption completed before the child turned 16. A guardianship order is not an adoption decree.

document_items.name: Legal Custody and Joint Residence Evidence
document_items.subtitle: Shows 2 years of legal custody and 2 years of living together in an adoption case

document_items.name: Custody Order or Other Parent's Consent
document_items.subtitle: May be asked for when the child's parents are divorced or separated, or the other parent has custody rights

document_items.name: Name Change or Identity Discrepancy Evidence
document_items.subtitle: Explains different names, spellings, or dates across the child's and the petitioner's records

document_items.name: Secondary Parent-Child Relationship Evidence
document_items.subtitle: Used when the birth record is unavailable, late-registered, or inconsistent (FRC, school, medical, vaccination records)

document_items.name: Record Unavailability Evidence
document_items.subtitle: Official explanation when a required civil record genuinely cannot be obtained

document_items.name: Certified English Translations
document_items.subtitle: Complete English translations of every submitted non-English document

document_items.name: Child's Passport
document_items.subtitle: The child's Pakistani passport, needed at the NVC and interview stages. Check the passport office's current rules for a minor's application.

document_items.name: Family Registration Certificate (FRC)
document_items.subtitle: NADRA family record, useful as supporting evidence and often asked for later

document_items.name: Police Character Certificate
document_items.subtitle: Pakistan Character Certificate from a Police Facilitation Center or local police office. Only if the child is 16 or older. Get it at the NVC stage, not now, so it is still valid at the interview.

document_items.name: Passport-Style Photos
document_items.subtitle: Needed later for the medical exam and the immigrant visa application

steps.pakistanSpecific: For Pakistani records, use documents from the competent issuing authority. The child's Birth Registration Certificate comes from the local Union Council, Municipal Corporation, CDA or Cantonment Board, and is the central IR-2 relationship document. The CRC (B-Form) and FRC are NADRA records: they support the birth certificate, and together with school, medical and vaccination records they can serve as alternate evidence where the birth record is late-registered, unavailable or inconsistent. For a Muslim marriage, the Marriage Registration Certificate (MRC) usually comes from the same local authority; for a non-Muslim marriage, the issuing authority depends on the religion and the local registration process. A Pakistani guardianship order is not automatically an adoption under U.S. immigration law; speak with a qualified U.S. immigration attorney before filing on that basis.

guide_steps.text:
USCIS no longer accepts personal/business checks, money orders, or cashier's checks. You must use one of the approved payment options:

  • Option C: If you cannot pay electronically, request an exemption from the electronic payment requirement with Form G-1651 (Exemption for Paper Fee Payment). This is not a fee waiver: the filing fee still has to be paid.
USCIS Form G-1651 Exemption Requirements
To request an exemption, you must certify that electronic payment and collection methods are not possible and you meet 1 or more of the following requirements:
  • You do not have access to banking services or electronic payment systems;
  • Electronic disbursement would cause you undue hardship (infrastructure barriers in remote/foreign areas or personal limitations), as discussed in 31 C.F.R. Part 208 (GovInfo Official Citation ↗);
  • Non-electronic transactions are necessary or desirable for national security or law enforcement reasons; or
  • There are other circumstances as determined by the secretary of the treasury, as reflected in regulations or other guidance.
Hardship categories under 31 C.F.R. Sec. 208.4: Infrastructure barriers (foreign/remote regions lacking U.S. digital banking) and personal barriers (financial, physical, or technical inability to manage online banking).
guide_steps.note: Download and print Form G-1450, Form G-1650, or Form G-1651 from uscis.gov and fill it out completely before placing it in the packet.

tool_data.title: USCIS Notice Received
tool_data.subtitle: USCIS may ask for additional evidence or information before deciding your petition. Identify the notice type below so Rahvana can guide your response.

alert.heading: Do not ignore this notice
alert.body: Missing the response deadline can result in your petition being denied, including denial based on abandonment. USCIS generally does not grant extensions beyond the permitted response period.

intro_card.heading: Receiving a USCIS notice is not the end of the road
intro_card.body: Most notices give you an opportunity to respond before a final decision is made. The key is to read the notice carefully, respond to exactly what USCIS asked for, and submit a complete response before the deadline.

notice_types.label: I-797, Approval Notice
notice_types.description: USCIS has approved your I-130 petition and issued an I-797 approval notice. Save the original notice and prepare for the NVC stage.

notice_types.label: RFE, Request for Evidence
notice_types.description: USCIS needs additional evidence or information before it can decide your petition. This is the most common notice. Receiving an RFE does not mean your petition has been denied.

notice_types.label: RFI, Request for Additional Information
notice_types.description: USCIS is asking for clarifying information. Similar in nature to an RFE but typically more limited in scope.

notice_types.label: RFO, Request for Original Document
notice_types.description: USCIS is requesting an original document. You may have submitted a copy where an original is required.

notice_types.label: NOID, Notice of Intent to Deny
notice_types.description: USCIS is considering denying your petition and is giving you a chance to respond. This is more serious than an RFE. Consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

notice_types.label: Denial, I-130 Petition Denied
notice_types.description: USCIS has issued a denial of your I-130 petition. Review the denial notice carefully, it explains the reasons and your available options such as appeal or motion.

notice_types.label: Other USCIS notice or request
notice_types.description: USCIS may send other types of requests such as biometrics appointments or interview notices. Follow the specific instructions on your notice.

where_to_find.title: Where to find your notice

items.detail: Log in to my.uscis.gov and check your case notices and messages. USCIS recommends checking your online account first.
Notices may also be sent by mail to the petitioner's address on file. Keep your address updated with USCIS.

where_to_find.note: If your USCIS online account shows an RFE, an online response portal may be available. Do not mail a duplicate response if you submit online.

deadline_warning.heading: Check the deadline on your actual notice
deadline_warning.body: Do not assume you have a specific number of days. The deadline printed on your notice always controls. For an RFE, the maximum response period is up to 12 weeks; for a NOID, it is up to 30 days. These are maximums, not a guaranteed amount of time.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Evidence · Prepare & submit response
steps.step_description: USCIS may issue a Request for Evidence (RFE) or Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) if additional information or documents are needed. Respond fully before the stated deadline.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFE
guide_data.subtitle: A Request for Evidence (RFE) means USCIS needs more information before deciding your child petition. This is your opportunity to provide the evidence that closes the gap.

alert.heading: An RFE does not mean your petition was denied
alert.body: Receiving an RFE means USCIS is giving you a chance to provide additional evidence before making a final decision. Many child petitions are approved after a successful RFE response.

warning_banner.text: Submit your complete RFE response before the deadline printed on your notice. Do not send documents in pieces, USCIS treats a partial response as a request for a decision on the existing record.

common_rfe_reasons.title: Common reasons USCIS issues an IR-2 child I-130 RFE
common_rfe_reasons.subtitle: Read your RFE notice first to identify exactly what USCIS is requesting. The categories below describe common areas for child petitions, your response should address your specific notice, not all of these.

categories.label: Proof of qualifying parent-child relationship
categories.description: USCIS may require stronger evidence establishing the legal parent-child relationship between the U.S. citizen petitioner and the child beneficiary.
evidence_examples: Child's official birth certificate naming the petitioner as a parent
Mother petitioning: child's birth certificate showing the mother's name
Father petitioning (parents married): child's birth certificate + parents' marriage certificate (Nikah Nama & MRC)
Father petitioning (parents not married): proof of legitimation, or evidence of a genuine father-child relationship
Stepparent petitioning: marriage certificate showing the marriage to the child's parent took place before the child turned 18
Adoptive parent petitioning: adoption decree from before the child turned 16 + proof of 2 years of legal custody and joint residence
NADRA Child Registration Certificate (CRC / B-Form) and Family Registration Certificate (FRC)
DNA relationship testing (only if explicitly requested or suggested by USCIS from an AABB-accredited lab)
categories.important_note: Do not automatically send all of these. Read exactly what your RFE requests and provide evidence relevant to that specific relationship type.

categories.label: Missing, incomplete, or secondary civil documentation
categories.description: USCIS may determine that submitted birth or marriage documentation is insufficient, late-registered, or missing required civil registration details.
evidence_examples: Union Council / relevant local government Birth Registration Certificate. A NADRA CRC (B-Form) or FRC may also be used as supporting or alternate civil documentation, as applicable.
Certified English translations with translator certification
Secondary evidence for a late-registered birth (school, vaccination, or hospital records)
Affidavits of birth from older relatives with personal knowledge of the birth
NADRA Family Registration Certificate (FRC)
categories.important_note: For Pakistani civil documents, USCIS may ask for the local-authority birth or marriage registration certificate, NADRA records such as the CRC or FRC, certified English translations, and secondary birth evidence if the birth was registered late.

categories.label: Petitioner citizenship verification
categories.description: USCIS may request additional proof that the petitioner is a U.S. citizen.
evidence_examples: Unexpired U.S. passport (copy of all biographical pages)
Certificate of Naturalization or Certificate of Citizenship
U.S. Birth Certificate (if born in the United States)
Consular Report of Birth Abroad (CRBA)

categories.label: Inconsistencies across documents
categories.description: If names, parent names, or dates of birth differ across documents (such as the child's birth certificate, CRC, FRC, passport, and Form I-130), USCIS may request clarification.
evidence_examples: Explanation letter addressing specific discrepancies
One and the same affidavit explaining name spelling variations
Certified civil or NADRA correction records
Official legal name change documentation
categories.important_note: Name spelling variations and date discrepancies across Pakistani identity documents (CRC, CNIC, passport, Nikah Nama, FRC) are common. Address each discrepancy directly and specifically.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Don't panic, read your RFE first
guide_steps.text: An RFE does not mean your petition is denied. USCIS is asking for additional evidence before making a decision. Your first task is to obtain the actual RFE notice and read it carefully, every word of it.
guide_steps.note: Get the notice from your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or from physical mail. The online account is the recommended first place to check.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Identify exactly what USCIS is requesting
guide_steps.text: Do not randomly gather documents. The RFE will specifically identify what is deficient and what USCIS needs. Your response must directly address the specific issue identified in the RFE, nothing more, nothing less.
guide_steps.note: For example: 'Submit evidence demonstrating the parent-child relationship between petitioner and beneficiary' is different from 'Submit a certified English translation of the birth certificate.' Each requires a different response.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Check the deadline printed on your notice
guide_steps.text: The response deadline is printed on your RFE notice. Do not assume you have a specific number of days, the actual notice controls your deadline. USCIS policy states that extensions beyond the permitted response period are generally not granted.
guide_steps.note: Mark the deadline in your calendar immediately. Build in time to organize, review, and submit your response well before the deadline.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Organize your evidence by RFE request
guide_steps.text: Structure your evidence to match each item USCIS requested. Group documents under the specific request they address. For example, USCIS Request: Proof of parent-child relationship: Exhibit A, child's Birth Registration Certificate, Exhibit B, parents' Nikah Nama & MRC, Exhibit C, Child Registration Certificate (CRC), Exhibit D, Family Registration Certificate (FRC). This structure makes it easy for the USCIS officer to match your response to their request.
guide_steps.note: Clear organization significantly helps the reviewing officer understand your response and reduces the chance of important evidence being overlooked.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 5
guide_steps.title: Write a cover letter
guide_steps.text: Prepare a brief cover letter that explains: (1) what USCIS requested, (2) how your response addresses each specific request, and (3) what evidence is included and how it is organized. The cover letter is the roadmap for your response package.
guide_steps.note: The cover letter does not need to be lengthy. It should clearly summarize the response contents and make it easy for the officer to navigate your package.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 6
guide_steps.title: Assemble one complete response package
guide_steps.text: Gather your cover letter and all evidence together into one complete response package before submitting. USCIS policy states that when responding to an RFE, materials should generally be submitted together. A partial response is treated as a request for a decision on the record, USCIS does not wait for additional packages or issue another RFE.
guide_steps.note: Double-check that every document is included, every translation is certified, and the cover letter is accurate before you submit.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 7
guide_steps.title: Choose the correct submission method
guide_steps.text: Check whether your USCIS online account provides an RFE response portal for your case. If it does, follow the online submission instructions. If your case requires a mailed response, use the address and instructions specified in your RFE notice.
guide_steps.note: USCIS has specifically stated that users who respond online should NOT also mail a duplicate response. Follow the method indicated on your notice or in your USCIS account.

guide_steps.label: RFE Response · Step 8
guide_steps.title: Keep a complete copy of everything you submit
guide_steps.text: Before submitting, make copies of your complete response package, including the cover letter and all evidence. If submitting by mail, use a trackable carrier and save the tracking number. If submitting online, save a copy of the confirmation.
guide_steps.note: Your copy of the response is important if questions arise later about what was submitted and when.

citations.text: USCIS Policy Manual - Request For Evidence

after_submission.heading: After you submit your RFE response
after_submission.body: Your case returns to USCIS review. USCIS will consider the submitted evidence and issue one of these outcomes.

outcomes.label: Approval
outcomes.description: USCIS approves the I-130 petition. For consular processing, the case moves toward the National Visa Center (NVC) stage.

outcomes.label: Denial
outcomes.description: If the response does not establish eligibility, USCIS may deny the petition. The denial notice will explain available appeal and motion options.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If your RFE involves complex legal issues or you are uncertain how to respond, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Additional Information · Prepare & submit response
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Request for Additional Information (RFI) on your I-130 petition. An RFI requests additional or clarifying information. Read the actual notice to determine exactly what USCIS requires and the applicable deadline.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFI
guide_data.subtitle: A Request for Additional Information (RFI) means USCIS needs specific clarifying information before proceeding. Read the notice carefully and respond directly to what is asked.

alert.heading: An RFI does not mean your petition was denied
alert.body: USCIS is requesting clarifying information to continue processing your petition. Respond to exactly what is asked, before the deadline printed on the notice.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Obtain and read the RFI notice
guide_steps.text: Check your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or your physical mail for the RFI notice. Read the notice carefully to understand exactly what information USCIS is requesting.
guide_steps.note: Read the actual notice to see exactly what USCIS requires and the deadline. Do not assume an RFI is smaller or less serious than an RFE.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline
guide_steps.text: The deadline is printed on your RFI notice. Note it immediately and plan your response with enough time to review everything before submitting.
guide_steps.note: USCIS generally does not grant extensions beyond the permitted response period. Missing the deadline can result in a denial.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Prepare a clear, direct response
guide_steps.text: Respond directly to the information USCIS requested. Provide only what is asked, clear, focused, and accurate. Include a brief cover letter that identifies what was requested and how your response addresses it.
guide_steps.note: Clarity is key. A focused response that directly answers the question is more effective than a large unorganized package.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Submit one complete response
guide_steps.text: Assemble your complete response into a single submission. Do not submit in pieces. Use the submission method specified in your RFI notice, online portal if available in your USCIS account, or mail if instructed.
guide_steps.note: If submitting online, do not also mail a duplicate response. Keep a copy of everything you submit.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If you are uncertain about your RFI response, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Original Document · Locate & submit original
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Request for an Original (RFO) document. USCIS is requesting that you submit the original version of a document you may have previously submitted as a copy.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFO
guide_data.subtitle: USCIS is requesting an original document. Identify the specific document requested, locate the original, and submit it following the instructions on your notice.

alert.heading: USCIS is asking for an original, not a copy
alert.body: Carefully read your RFO notice to identify exactly which document is required in original form. Submitting another copy will not satisfy the request. Submit an original only when USCIS specifically requests it. Otherwise, follow the applicable photocopy requirements. Keep a copy of any original document you send.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Identify the specific document requested
guide_steps.text: Read your RFO notice carefully. USCIS will identify the specific document it is requesting in original form. Common examples include original birth certificates, original marriage certificates/Nikah Namas, or other original civil documents.
guide_steps.note: If you are unsure whether your document is truly the original versus a certified copy, contact the issuing authority to clarify.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline
guide_steps.text: The deadline is printed on your RFO notice. Mark it immediately. Plan enough time to locate the document, make a copy for your records, and prepare your submission.
guide_steps.note: Do not wait until close to the deadline. Locating original documents, especially civil documents from Pakistan, may take time.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Make a copy before submitting the original
guide_steps.text: Before sending any original document to USCIS, make a clear copy for your own records. USCIS receives many documents and originals are not always returned promptly, or may take significant time to be returned.
guide_steps.note: Keep your copy in a safe place. If the original is irreplaceable, consider consulting an immigration attorney about the best approach.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Submit using a secure, trackable method
guide_steps.text: Send the original document using a secure and trackable shipping method. Include a cover letter identifying the case receipt number, the RFO reference, and what document is enclosed. Follow the submission instructions in your RFO notice.
guide_steps.note: Keep the tracking number and delivery confirmation. Once the carrier shows delivered, save that proof.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If you have concerns about submitting irreplaceable original documents, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Notice of Intent to Deny · Respond carefully before deadline
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) on your I-130 petition. A NOID is more serious than an RFE, USCIS is indicating it is considering denying your petition based on the current record and has provided an opportunity to respond before making a final decision.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS NOID
guide_data.subtitle: A Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) means USCIS is considering denying your petition. This is your opportunity to respond with evidence and legal arguments before a final decision is made.

alert.heading: A NOID is more serious than an RFE
alert.body: USCIS is not simply asking for more evidence. It is indicating that based on the current record, it intends to deny your petition, and has provided an opportunity to respond before making a final decision. Carefully review the reasons USCIS has stated. Because the response may require legal analysis, strongly consider getting help from a qualified immigration attorney.

noid_vs_rfe.title: NOID vs. RFE, the key difference

rfe.label: RFE
rfe.description: We need more evidence before we can make a decision.

noid.label: NOID
noid.description: Based on what we currently have, we are considering denying your petition. Here is why. You have an opportunity to respond before we make a final decision.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Obtain and read the NOID notice immediately
guide_steps.text: Obtain the NOID notice from your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or from physical mail. Read the entire notice carefully. USCIS is required to identify the intended reasons for denial, explain deficiencies, and identify potentially missing evidence.
guide_steps.note: Understanding exactly what USCIS says is wrong is the foundation of your response. Do not skip or skim any part of the notice.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline immediately
guide_steps.text: The response deadline is printed on your NOID notice. Note it immediately and treat it as your hard deadline. For a NOID the maximum response period is up to 30 days, much shorter than an RFE, and the date on your notice controls. Extensions are generally not granted.
guide_steps.note: Given the seriousness of a NOID, you should begin working on your response immediately, do not wait until close to the deadline.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney
guide_steps.text: Because a NOID response may require legal analysis and argumentation, not just evidence submission, strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney before preparing your response. An attorney can assess the specific deficiencies USCIS identified and advise on the best response strategy.
guide_steps.note: This is Rahvana's strongest recommendation for NOID situations. The consequences of a denial are significant, the response deserves careful legal attention.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Address each stated reason for the proposed denial
guide_steps.text: Your response must directly address each reason USCIS stated in the NOID. For each issue identified, explain why that reason does not support denial and provide evidence that counters or clarifies the issue.
guide_steps.note: A NOID response is not just an evidence package, it should include a legal argument explaining why, based on the law and facts, the petition should be approved.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 5
guide_steps.title: Submit one complete response before the deadline
guide_steps.text: Assemble your complete response, cover letter, legal arguments, and all supporting evidence, into a single submission. Follow the submission instructions on your NOID notice. Do not send documents in pieces.
guide_steps.note: Keep a complete copy of everything you submit, with proof of submission (tracking number or online confirmation).

after_noid_response.heading: After submitting your NOID response
after_noid_response.body: USCIS will review your response and issue a final decision.

outcomes.label: Approval
outcomes.description: USCIS approves the petition based on your response. The case moves toward the NVC stage for consular processing.

outcomes.label: Denial
outcomes.description: If the response does not establish eligibility, USCIS will deny the petition. The denial notice will explain available appeal and motion options such as an appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals.

citations.text: USCIS Policy Manual - Notice of Intent to Deny

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. A NOID is a serious notice that may require legal analysis. Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_description: USCIS has denied the I-130 petition. Review the denial notice carefully to understand the specific reasons and determine which options, appeal, motion, or another strategy, may be appropriate for your situation.

guide_data.title: I-130 Denied, Review Your Options
guide_data.subtitle: An I-130 denial is a serious outcome, but it may not be the end of the road. Review the denial notice carefully and understand what options may be available.

alert.heading: Carefully review the denial notice
alert.body: The denial notice explains USCIS's specific reasons for the denial and states what appeal or motion options are available in your case. The correct next step depends entirely on the specific reasons for the denial and the facts of your case. Do not file an appeal or motion without understanding the denial first.

denial_options.title: Possible options after an I-130 denial
denial_options.subtitle: Which option is appropriate depends on the specific reasons for the denial and the circumstances of your case. The denial notice itself explains what options are available.

options.label: Appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA)
options.description: Certain I-130 decisions can be appealed to the Board of Immigration Appeals using Form EOIR-29 (Notice of Appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals from a Decision of a DHS Officer). USCIS confirms that I-130 appeals are among the appeals filed using Form EOIR-29.
options.important: Appeals have strict deadlines. Form EOIR-29 is used for eligible appeals of DHS decisions, and it must be filed with the DHS/USCIS office named in the denial notice and the form instructions, not mailed directly to the BIA. Confirm the deadline and filing requirements in your denial notice and the current EOIR-29 instructions.

options.label: Motion to Reopen
options.description: A motion to reopen asks USCIS to reopen the case based on new facts or evidence that was not available at the time of the decision.
options.important: A motion to reopen is appropriate when there is new factual evidence that was not part of the original record. Review the denial carefully before pursuing this option.

options.label: Motion to Reconsider
options.description: A motion to reconsider asks USCIS to reconsider its decision based on an error of law or incorrect application of policy to the existing facts.
options.important: A motion to reconsider is appropriate when you believe USCIS made a legal error in the denial, not when you simply have new evidence.

options.label: File a new petition
options.description: Depending on the denial reason, it may sometimes be appropriate to file a new I-130 petition with corrected information or additional evidence. This should be carefully evaluated based on the specific denial reason.
options.important: Filing a new petition when an appeal or motion is more appropriate may not be the best strategy. Consult an immigration attorney.

attorney_recommendation.heading: Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney
attorney_recommendation.body: Determining the right strategy after an I-130 denial, appeal vs. motion vs. new petition, requires careful analysis of the denial reasons, the evidence record, and the applicable law. The wrong choice can waste time, resources, or foreclose other options. An experienced immigration attorney can help you evaluate the best path forward.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Read the denial notice completely
guide_steps.text: The denial notice contains the specific reasons USCIS denied the petition and explains what appeal or motion rights are available. Read it completely before deciding on any next step.
guide_steps.note: The denial notice is the most important document at this stage. Every option you consider must be evaluated against the specific reasons stated in the notice.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Note any deadlines for appeal or motion
guide_steps.text: If the denial notice indicates appeal or motion rights, it will also state the deadlines for filing. These deadlines are strict, missing them can eliminate certain options.
guide_steps.note: Do not delay in reviewing the notice and understanding the available deadlines. Begin consulting an attorney as soon as possible if you are considering an appeal or motion.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Consult a qualified immigration attorney
guide_steps.text: Given the complexity of determining the right post-denial strategy, consulting a qualified immigration attorney is strongly recommended. An attorney can review the denial notice, assess the options, and advise on the best course of action specific to your case.
guide_steps.note: Do not treat this as optional. The stakes of an I-130 denial are high, and the correct path forward requires professional evaluation.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Evaluate and act on the appropriate option
guide_steps.text: Based on the denial reasons and legal advice, determine whether an appeal (Form EOIR-29 to the BIA), a motion to reopen, a motion to reconsider, or another strategy is appropriate. Act within the applicable deadlines.
guide_steps.note: Rahvana can guide you through general information about each option, but the final decision on which path to take should be made with qualified legal assistance.

citations.text: Form EOIR-29, Notice of Appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. An I-130 denial requires careful legal analysis. Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney before taking any action.

steps.step_short_description: General notice guidance · Biometrics, interview, or appointment
steps.step_description: USCIS may send notices that are not standard evidence requests, such as appointment notices (Form I-797C), interview notices, transfer notices, or fee adjustment requests. Follow these universal steps to respond appropriately.

guide_data.title: Respond to Other USCIS Notice or Request
guide_data.subtitle: USCIS issues various types of notices during petition processing. Identify your specific notice type, follow the required instructions, and ensure timely compliance.

alert.heading: Identify the Form Number and Heading
alert.body: Official USCIS notices are usually issued on Form I-797C (Notice of Action) or Form I-797. Look at the top-right header and notice type line to understand whether action is required or if it is purely informational.

common_rfe_reasons.title: Common notice types you may receive
common_rfe_reasons.subtitle: USCIS sends several standard communication types. Find your notice type below:

categories.label: Biometrics / ASC Appointment Notice (Form I-797C)
categories.description: USCIS schedules an appointment at an Application Support Center (ASC) to capture fingerprints, photo, and signature. This is common if biometric verification is needed.
evidence_examples: Bring the original appointment notice with barcode.
Bring government-issued photo ID (valid passport, driver's license).
If you cannot attend, follow the reschedule instructions on the notice immediately before the appointment date.
categories.important_note: Failing to appear for a biometrics appointment without rescheduling can result in petition abandonment and denial.

categories.label: Interview Notice (Form I-797C)
categories.description: While most consular I-130 petitions are decided without an in-person USCIS interview, USCIS occasionally requests a petitioner interview.
evidence_examples: Original civil documents (child's birth certificate, parents' marriage certificate).
Relationship evidence that fits your case and the items listed on the interview notice (for example, father-child relationship evidence when that is the basis of the petition).
Valid government-issued photo identification.
categories.important_note: Carefully review the checklist of items to bring on the interview notice, and follow the arrival instructions on your appointment notice.

categories.label: Service Center Transfer Notice (Form I-797C)
categories.description: USCIS frequently transfers cases between service centers (e.g., Nebraska, Texas, Potomac, California, Vermont) to balance processing workloads across the agency.
evidence_examples: No action is required on your part.
Your receipt number remains unchanged.
Follow the transfer notice and continue monitoring your case through USCIS.
categories.important_note: A case transfer does not mean anything is wrong with your petition. It is routine workload management by USCIS.

categories.label: Fee Correction / Rejection Notice
categories.description: If payment could not be processed or an essential document was missing at intake, USCIS issues a notice explaining the intake issue.
evidence_examples: Check the specific rejection reason printed on the notice.
Submit corrected fee payment or missing signature promptly.

Pay with a valid electronic method: Form G-1450 (credit or debit card) or Form G-1650 (ACH from a U.S. bank account). If you cannot pay electronically, Form G-1651 requests an exemption from the electronic payment requirement; it is not a fee waiver.
categories.important_note: Pay close attention to any refiling instructions and deadline dates provided on the notice.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Read the entire notice thoroughly
guide_steps.text: Check the notice type in the header, read all instructions, and verify whether USCIS requires a response, an appearance, or if the notice is purely informational.
guide_steps.note: Look for specific keywords such as 'Action Required', 'Notice of Action', or 'Appointment Scheduled'.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check your USCIS online account
guide_steps.text: Log in to my.uscis.gov and check the 'Documents' tab for an electronic PDF copy of the notice. Online notices are often available days before physical mail arrives.
guide_steps.note: Ensure your mailing address in your USCIS account is completely accurate and up to date.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Note any deadlines or appointment dates
guide_steps.text: If the notice specifies an appointment date, time, and location, or gives a deadline to submit documents, mark it on your calendar immediately.
guide_steps.note: Never wait until the last week. If rescheduling is needed, USCIS generally requires requests to be submitted well ahead of the appointment date.

guide_steps.label: General Notice · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Comply with the exact instructions and retain proof
guide_steps.text: Attend the appointment or submit the requested documentation according to the exact mailing or online upload instructions. Keep copies of everything submitted, along with delivery tracking numbers or stamped appointment notices.
guide_steps.note: Save your stamped biometrics confirmation sheet or mailing receipt in your immigration records binder.

citations.text: USCIS Change of Address Online (Form AR-11)

actions: Review the NVC required civil document checklist for the IR-2 child category

tool_data.title: Prepare Civil Documents
tool_data.subtitle: Review and prepare the civil documents needed for the IR-2 child beneficiary's NVC / CEAC upload and consular interview readiness.

items.title: Child Beneficiary Passport Biographic Page
items.sub: Current passport page showing the child's photo, full name, date of birth, and nationality

sections.c: Upload a clear, high-resolution color scan of the biographic data page of the child beneficiary's current, unexpired passport. All four corners must be visible with no glare or obstruction.
The passport must be valid for at least six months beyond the child's intended date of entry into the United States. If the passport will expire soon, renew it prior to the immigrant visa interview.
The child's name, date of birth, place of birth, and parents' names in the passport must match Form DS-260, the Form I-130 petition, and Pakistan NADRA civil records exactly.

items.title: Child Beneficiary Birth Certificate
items.sub: Computerized Birth Registration Certificate from the Union Council, Municipal Corporation, CDA or Cantonment Board

sections.c: Submit the child's computerized Birth Registration Certificate from the local Union Council, Municipal Corporation, CDA or Cantonment Board, with a certified English translation if it is not in English. A NADRA CRC (B-Form) or FRC supports it but does not replace it. The certificate must clearly list the child's full name, exact date and place of birth, and the full names of both biological parents.

If the birth was registered more than one year after the date of birth, consular officers at Embassy Islamabad will scrutinize the record. Submit secondary contemporaneous evidence such as hospital birth records, school leaving certificates, or childhood vaccination records.

Under the U.S. Department of State Reciprocity Schedule for Pakistan, hospital birth slips alone are not acceptable civil documents. An official Union Council / Cantonment Board registration certificate is mandatory.

items.title: NADRA Child Registration Certificate (CRC / B-Form) or FRC
items.sub: Official NADRA family registry document showing parent-child relationship

sections.c: The NADRA Child Registration Certificate (CRC, commonly known as the B-Form for minors) or Family Registration Certificate (FRC with parents) officially verifies the child's registration under their parents in Pakistan's national civil database.

sections.t: Why U.S. Embassy Islamabad requires it
sections.c: Consular officers at Embassy Islamabad routinely request the NADRA CRC or FRC to corroborate birth certificates and confirm lawful family composition, preventing identity fraud.
Ensure the NADRA CRC/B-Form is in English or accompanied by a certified English translation. Verify that the parent CNIC numbers and child's date of birth match all other submitted records.

items.title: Passport-Style Photographs (2x2 Inches)
items.sub: Two identical recent color photographs of the child meeting State Department standards

sections.c: Two identical 2 x 2 inch (51 x 51 mm) color photos taken within the last 6 months against a plain white or off-white background. The child must have a neutral facial expression with both eyes open, facing directly toward the camera.

No other person should appear in the photo. For infants, the child may be placed on a plain white sheet or in a car seat covered with a white sheet. Eyes must be open for the shot, but minor head tilt is acceptable for very young babies.
Eyeglasses are not allowed. Head coverings are permitted only for religious reasons, and the full face from forehead to chin must remain completely visible.

items.title: Police Certificate (Ages 16+ Only)
items.sub: Pakistan Police Character Certificate from PKM; children under 16 are completely EXEMPT

sections.c: IMPORTANT: Under U.S. Department of State regulations (9 FAM 504.4-4(B)), children under 16 years of age are NOT required to submit police certificates. If your child is 15 or younger, this requirement is waived.

If the child has reached their 16th birthday, a Police Character Certificate is required from Pakistan (obtained through Police Khidmat Markaz - PKM) and from any country of nationality or residence where the youth has resided for 6 months or more after age 16.
Police certificates are valid for two years for U.S. immigrant visa processing. Ensure the certificate remains unexpired through the consular interview date at Embassy Islamabad.

items.title: Petitioner's Proof of U.S. Citizenship
items.sub: U.S. passport, Certificate of Naturalization, Certificate of Citizenship, or U.S. birth certificate

sections.c: The IR-2 visa category is exclusively for children of U.S. citizens. Proof of petitioner's citizenship confirms qualification for IR-2 classification and establishes eligibility for automatic citizenship under INA Section 320 upon admission.
Upload a color copy of the petitioner's unexpired U.S. passport biographic page, U.S. birth certificate, Certificate of Naturalization, or Certificate of Citizenship.

items.title: Parents' Marriage Certificate (Nikah Nama & MRC)
items.sub: Required if child was born to married parents or if father is petitioning

sections.c: Required if the child was born during the parents' marriage, or if a biological father is petitioning for a child born of a lawful marriage in Pakistan.

Submit the Nikah Nama with a certified English translation and the computerized Marriage Registration Certificate (MRC). For a Muslim marriage, the MRC usually comes from the local Union Council, Municipal Corporation, CDA or Cantonment Board; for a non-Muslim marriage, the issuing authority depends on the religion and the local registration process.

items.title: Legitimation or Bona Fide Father-Child Relationship Evidence
items.sub: Required if child was born out of wedlock and biological father is petitioning

sections.c: If the child was born out of wedlock to a U.S. citizen father, INA Section 101(b)(1)(C) or (D) requires proof that the child was legitimated before age 18, or that a bona fide parent-child emotional or financial relationship was established before the child turned 21.
Submit proof of emotional/financial support: money remittance receipts, school fee payments, medical bills, joint photos over the years, communication logs, and sworn affidavits from relatives.

items.title: Stepparent Marriage and Relationship Records
items.sub: Required if petition is filed by a stepparent; marriage must have occurred before child's 18th birthday

sections.c: Under INA Section 101(b)(1)(B), a stepchild relationship exists only if the marriage creating the relationship occurred before the child reached 18 years of age. Submit the marriage certificate proving the date.
Submit official divorce decrees, annulments, or death certificates proving the legal termination of all prior marriages for both the stepparent and the biological parent.

items.title: Adoption Decree, Legal Custody, and 2-Year Joint Residence
items.sub: Required if child is adopted; adoption must be finalized before age 16 with 2 years legal/physical custody

sections.c: The child must have been adopted before age 16 (or before 18 if adopted alongside a biological sibling under 16). The adoptive U.S. citizen parent must demonstrate at least 2 years of legal custody and 2 years of joint physical residence with the child.
Certified copy of the final adoption court decree, guardianship orders, school records, rental agreements, or utility records proving 2 years of joint cohabitation.

items.title: Legal Custody Decree or Non-Accompanying Parent Consent Letter (NOC)
items.sub: Required for minor children travelling without one biological parent

sections.c: When a minor child (under age 18) immigrates without one of their biological parents, U.S. Embassy Islamabad strictly enforces child protection and parental rights standards.

Submit a certified family court custody decree awarding sole legal custody to the petitioning/accompanying parent, or an official notarized No Objection Certificate (NOC) / Affidavit of Consent signed by the non-accompanying biological parent with a copy of their CNIC or passport.
If the other biological parent is deceased, upload their official Union Council / NADRA death certificate with certified English translation.

items.title: Name Change or Identity Discrepancy Documents
items.sub: Required if child's or parent's name differs across submitted records

sections.c: If the child's name, parents' names, or dates of birth differ between the birth certificate, passport, B-Form, or petition, provide official documentation explaining the discrepancy.
Official court name change decree, NADRA revised registration certificate, gazette notification, or sworn one-and-the-same person affidavit.

items.title: Court and Juvenile Records
items.sub: Required if beneficiary has ever been arrested, charged, or convicted of an offense

sections.c: If the beneficiary (typically older youths aged 16+) has ever been arrested, cited, charged, or convicted anywhere in the world, even if records were expunged or dismissed.
Certified copies of police reports, court complaints, plea agreements, final judgments, and sentencing or rehabilitation records with certified English translations.

items.title: Military or Service Records
items.sub: Required if the child beneficiary has served in any military or armed forces

sections.c: Only applies if the beneficiary (ages 17+) has served in any military or defense force. Upload a certified copy of the service record, discharge book, or release certificate.

items.title: Missing Document / Record Unavailability Evidence
items.sub: Required if any primary civil record cannot be obtained

sections.c: Obtain an official Certificate of Non-Availability from the competent Union Council or civil registrar stating that the record does not exist after a diligent search.
Submit strong secondary evidence such as hospital birth records, school certificates, baptismal records, and sworn affidavits from relatives with personal knowledge of the event.

items.title: Organized Certified English Translations
items.sub: Translations with certificate of accuracy for every Urdu civil document

sections.c: Any document not in English must be accompanied by a full English translation. The translator must sign a certification statement confirming they are competent to translate and that the translation is accurate and complete.
Common documents needing certified translation include Urdu Nikah Nama, Union Council birth records, court decrees, and custody affidavits.

items.title: Upload-Ready Digital Scans (<2 MB)
items.sub: Clean, color PDF or JPEG scans formatted for CEAC upload

sections.c: Files must be in PDF or JPEG format, under 2 MB each (or CEAC current maximum). Color scans are strongly recommended. Both front and back of multi-page documents must be scanned and merged into a single multi-page PDF.

items.title: Interview Originals and Certified Copies Set
items.sub: Physical folder of original documents ready for Embassy Islamabad interview

sections.c: Even though documents are submitted electronically to CEAC, consular officers at U.S. Embassy Islamabad require the applicant to bring original or certified copies of all civil documents, NADRA certificates, consent letters, and translations to the interview.
